where: Exam traps, third bullet (mixing up absorbance and transmittance)
problem: The trap says doubling concentration 'halves T'. That is only true when the starting transmittance happens to be 0.50. In general, if A doubles then T is squared, not halved: T_new = 10^(−2A) = (T_old)². For example, A going from 0.10 to 0.20 takes T from 0.79 to 0.63, not to 0.40. A student who memorises 'doubling c halves T' will get numerical questions wrong.
fix: A is logarithmic, so doubling concentration doubles A but squares T: if A goes from 0.30 to 0.60, T falls from 0.50 to 0.25. The halving seen in that one example is not a general rule. Both relations hold only inside the linear range.

where: Exam traps, fourth bullet (glass cuvette for UV)
problem: The reason given is incomplete and can mislead. If the blank is also in a glass cuvette, the glass absorption is cancelled by blanking (A = 0 is set with glass in the beam); the real trouble is that almost no UV reaches the detector, so noise and stray light make the reading unreliable. Absorbance reads falsely high only when the sample cell is glass and the blank is quartz.
fix: Glass absorbs UV strongly below about 340 nm, so the light reaching the detector is very weak and the reading becomes noisy and stray-light distorted. If the sample is in glass while the blank is quartz, the extra absorption is added to the sample and A reads falsely high. Use quartz (or UV-transparent plastic) cuvettes for both blank and sample in UV work.

problem: The last clause is muddled: 'each factor of 3 in concentration multiplies the old transmittance by 10^(−A_old) again' mixes two symbols for the same quantity and reads as if the concentration were tripled several times. It is also unclearly worded for a second-language reader.
fix: A becomes three times its old value (A_new = 3A_old) because A = εcl. Transmittance becomes the cube of its old value: T_new = 10^(−3A_old) = (10^(−A_old))³ = (T_old)³, that is T_old × T_old × T_old.
